$comment: The intent corpus, and the only file in this directory the agent is ever shown.
Every case is one user's opening message to `bmad-tea`, written the way a person writes it rather than the way
the menu describes itself. Not one of them quotes a menu code, a workflow name, or a trigger phrase out of a
workflow's frontmatter, because a corpus that does is measuring string matching and reporting it as routing.
The four ambiguous intents are ambiguous from what the agent is shown, which is this file plus SKILL.md and
customize.toml. An intent whose second reading only opens once you have read a workflow's frontmatter or the
knowledge index is not ambiguous to the agent, and scoring it as a clarification measures a fact the agent was
never given.
The answers live in ground-truth.json and never enter a prompt. test/eval-bmad-tea-routing.js asserts that
separation on the assembled prompt before it spends a model call, the way test/eval-trace.js does.
`id` is the case id the manifest's caseCount is checked against and the id every stored replay case names.
The oracle for the routing corpus. The agent never sees this file, and the harness proves it: every key named
in GROUND_TRUTH_ONLY_KEYS is searched for in the assembled prompt before a model call is spent, and the whole
file's bytes are searched for too, the way test/eval-trace.js guards its own ground truth.
Where the three actions come from. `route` and `clarify` are Step 8 of src/agents/bmad-tea/SKILL.md verbatim:
dispatch a clear match directly, and pause to clarify only when two or more items are genuinely close. `decline`
is not. Step 8's third clause says that when nothing on the menu fits the agent should just continue the
conversation, and it names chat, clarifying questions and bmad-help as fair game. It forbids a dispatch and it
asks for no refusal. The requirement that an unservable intent be declined and that the answer name what is
missing comes from this suite's own exit condition in test/evals/suite-manifest.json, and the prompt states it
outright, so the agent is scored against a rule it was given rather than one inferred from a skill that does not
carry it. The prompt is the whole of what makes that fair, and if the skill is ever taught to decline in its own
words, this paragraph is where that should be recorded.
`expectedMenuCode` is the primary key because the menu is what the agent dispatches from. Nine of the ten items
name a skill and one, GATE, names a prompt, so `expectedWorkflow` is null there and is scored only where the menu
names a workflow. The harness checks every code and every workflow here against the live
src/agents/bmad-tea/customize.toml, so an edit to the menu fails this corpus rather than silently invalidating it.
`decidingTokens` is the deciding feature of the intent, written as words the user's own message carries. The
harness refuses a token that is not in the intent, and that rule is the whole reason the number means anything:
a token reachable only from the menu row the agent is being scored for choosing can be satisfied without reading
the message at all, which turns a grounding metric into a vocabulary metric. Containment is the score:
lowercase, a word boundary at the start of the token, and a prefix match after it, so `plan` counts `planned`.
That is deliberately mechanical. A stated reason judged by a model is a second eval with its own error rate
sitting inside this one.
`scopeTokens` is what the user named and what the dispatch has to still be about. The agent passes no scope
structurally, so the only observable is whether the answer restates it, and restating the whole message would
satisfy any token set, so the harness also bounds the length of an answer's scope against the message's.
`candidateCodes` is the set a clarifying question has to name. Asking 'which did you mean?' without saying between
what is not a clarification, it is a stall.
